title: Spontaneous composition, piano fingering and throwing music away
summary: His own piano fingering system, discarding pieces, and notating the six-eight theme of Revelations in four-four.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You once described yourself as a spontaneous composer.
Well, every second I'm not that, but every now and then I sit down at a piano and do some thing --- it

comes to my head, and not miss too many notes, I get away with it. On bass -- I'm talking about piano because my schooling was not that hip on piano. It was all my own fingering, most of it. I studied jazz piano with Lloyd Reese, and the scales weren't that hard, the scales. The proper fingering for the D minor or B minor because the fingering is different. I found my own system out, where the fingering was the same on the C scale as it was on the D flat scale. You can use the same fingers every time.
Yeah.
And I don't know how practical it is for anybody else, but I didn't think about the notes or what key I was in, when I did it that way. I just (inaudible) and play, by using the same fingers.
That makes a great deal of sense.
What?
It makes a lot of sense.
(inaudible) piano?
No, I never --
You never (inaudible) training, though.
Not much.
Spontaneous compositions. Maybe I can do eight bars (inaudible), but I think there are only so many of those you can do. And then they all end up sounding alike.
Yeah, you begin to look at yourself.

Yeah, you've got to sit down and study yourself and fool around in your head, what you want to play in your head and what you're able to play on the piano. At least, that's what I have to do, to get out of a rut.
Yeah.

I spend a whole lot of time just throwing away music. I found pieces I didn't like at all, and I wrote almost 24 bars, and never finished it, because I was trying to get out of something. Or I'd write something and at the Five Spot. finish it and leave it on the piano (inaudible). Like, I got two compositions -- I wrote my best compositions. One was called Dark Blackness and one was called Light Darkness. Light, you know. Dark Blackness, Dark Lightness, and Light Darkness. And it's something completely different, although most of my things are completely different. Maybe that's why, because of the stuff that I throw away in between gets rid of the connection.

Then there's a piece like Revelations, where I write every note and take my time, get everything down I wanted. And then turn around and do the six-eight, and do the same because of the notation, the guys don't even know it happened. thing in four-four. (Inaudible.) Have you seen that score?
I don't know if I have, no.
Well, ask Gunther Schuller (inaudible) to let you see it. Because when I first started that theme, (singing), six-eight theme, I didn't know it was possible to write it in four-four.
But I tried and got it done. Converted it and had it come out sounding the same.
Yeah.
Other than making it a swing beat Going Against It (inaudible).
